unit.title: Sound
unit.blurb: Vibrations, volume, pitch and sound insulators – and how musical instruments work.

O1.t: Explain that sounds are made by vibrations and travel through solids, liquids and gases, but not through empty space.

O2.t: Describe volume and pitch, and link them to the size and speed of vibrations.

O3.t: Describe how distance and sound insulators change the volume of a sound.

O4.t: Plan a fair test of materials as sound insulators and draw a conclusion.

O5.t: Explain how the length, tension and thickness of strings, and the length of tubes and bars, change pitch.

captions: Hello, sound scientists! Can you hear me? Great!
This is lesson 2.1: how sounds are made.
Try this right now. Put your hand gently on your throat.
Now hum your favourite song. Hmmmm.
Can you feel a tickly buzz? That is your voice box vibrating. Every sound is made by something vibrating.
To vibrate means to move backwards and forwards very quickly.
Put some rice on a drum, then hit the drum. Look! The rice jumps, because the drum skin is vibrating.
The vibrations pass through the air to your ear, and you hear the sound.
Pause and think. What must happen to make a sound?
Anything that makes a sound is called a sound source.
Pluck a guitar string, and it vibrates. Ring a bell, and the metal vibrates.
That annoying bzzz from a mosquito? Its wings vibrate hundreds of times every second!
Even a phone speaker has a part inside that vibrates to make music.
Sound needs something to travel through, called a medium.
Sound travels through gases like air, through liquids like water, and through solids like wood and metal.
Put your ear on a table and tap it. The sound is louder through the wood!
But in space there is no air, so there is no sound at all. Astronauts use radios to talk.
Did you know? Sound travels really well through water.
Some whale songs can be heard hundreds of kilometres away. That is the longest phone call in the sea!
Riddle time! In space, why can't anyone hear you sing, even if you sing really loudly?
Because there is no air in space to carry the vibrations!
Your turn. Can sound travel through a solid?
Let's build a string telephone.
Ask an adult to make a small hole in the bottom of two paper cups, and tie a long string between them.
Pull the string tight. One person talks into a cup, and the other listens.
The vibrations travel along the string! What happens if the string is loose?
Let's remember.
All sounds are made by vibrations.
To vibrate means to move backwards and forwards very quickly.
Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.
But sound cannot travel through empty space.
Sound-tastic work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello again, sound scientists! Shhh… or should I shout?
This is lesson 2.2: volume and pitch.
Volume is how loud or quiet a sound is.
Hit a drum hard, and the skin makes big vibrations. The sound is loud.
Tap it gently, and the vibrations are small. The sound is quiet.
Leaves rustling in the wind make a very quiet sound.
People talking make a medium sound.
A fire engine siren is very loud, so everyone can hear it coming.
Very loud sounds can damage your ears, so protect them with ear defenders.
Pause and think. How can you make a drum sound louder?
Pitch is how high or low a sound is.
A long, slow-vibrating string makes a low pitch, like a growly bear.
A short, fast-vibrating string makes a high pitch, like a squeaky mouse.
Let's listen to the animal choir. An elephant rumbles with a very low pitch.
A dog barks with a medium pitch.
A mouse squeaks with a high pitch.
And a bat makes sounds so high that our ears cannot hear them at all!
Did you know? Elephants make rumbles that are too low for people to hear.
But other elephants can hear them kilometres away. A secret elephant telephone!
Your turn. Which makes a higher pitch, a short string or a long string?
Scientists can see sounds on a computer as wavy lines.
A low pitch has waves that are far apart. A high pitch has waves that are close together.
A loud sound has tall waves.
And a quiet sound has short waves.
Let's make a rubber band guitar.
Stretch some rubber bands around an open box, and pluck each one.
Push a pencil under the bands to make the vibrating part shorter.
Listen carefully. Do shorter or tighter bands sound higher?
Let's remember.
Volume is how loud or quiet a sound is.
Big vibrations make loud sounds, and small vibrations make quiet sounds.
Pitch is how high or low a sound is.
Fast vibrations make a high pitch, and slow vibrations make a low pitch.
Brilliant listening! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, sound scientists! Are you ready for a noisy lesson?
This is lesson 2.3: changing the volume of sound.
Imagine an alarm clock ringing.
Now walk away from it.
Walk further, and further.
The sound gets quieter and quieter. The greater the distance from a sound source, the quieter it sounds.
We can also make a sound quieter by covering it.
Wrap the alarm clock in something soft, like foam, wool or a thick towel, and the sound is muffled.
Soft materials absorb the vibrations, like a sponge soaking up water. We call them sound insulators.
Pause and think. Why do soft materials make sounds quieter?
Sound insulators are used everywhere. Recording studios have bumpy foam on the walls, so there are no echoes.
People who work with loud machines wear ear defenders to protect their ears.
And homes near busy roads have double windows to keep the traffic noise outside.
Sometimes we want sounds to be louder. A megaphone points all the sound in one direction.
A guitar has a hollow body that makes the string's sound much louder.
Try cupping your hand behind your ear. Sounds seem louder! That is how big rabbit ears work.
Joke time! Why did the owl not want to go to the rock concert?
Because it didn't give a hoot about loud music!
Your turn. Which is the best sound insulator: foam, metal or glass?
Let's do a fair test of sound insulators.
Put a ringing timer in a box, and wrap it in one material, like foam, newspaper or bubble wrap.
Walk away slowly until you cannot hear it, and measure that distance.
Try each material in the same way. The shorter the distance, the better the insulator!
Let's remember.
Sounds get quieter the further away you are.
Soft materials absorb the vibrations.
Materials that muffle sound are called sound insulators.
And megaphones and hollow boxes make sounds louder.
Great work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, music makers! Let's turn this lesson into a band.
This is lesson 2.4: changing the pitch of sound.
String instruments, like guitars and violins, can change their pitch in three ways.
A shorter string vibrates faster, so the pitch is higher. Guitarists press the strings to make them shorter.
A tighter string has more tension, so the pitch is higher. That is what the tuning pegs do.
And a thinner string also makes a higher pitch.
Pause and think. How can you make a guitar string sound higher?
Let's make music with bottles of water.
If you tap the bottles, the one with the most water makes the lowest note, because more water vibrates more slowly.
But if you blow across the tops, the one with the most air makes the lowest note! The air inside is what vibrates.
Every instrument plays the same game. On a drum, a tighter skin makes a higher pitch.
In a trumpet, the player changes the length of the vibrating air in the tube. A shorter tube makes a higher pitch.
On a xylophone, the short bars make high notes, and the long bars make low notes.
Did you know? When a violin plays a high note, its string vibrates hundreds of times every second.
That is far too fast for your eyes to see. It just looks blurry!
Your turn. Which bar on a xylophone makes the lowest note?
Joke time! Why did the singer climb a ladder?
To reach the high notes!
Let's build a bottle xylophone.
Line up four bottles, and fill them with different amounts of water.
Tap each bottle gently with a metal spoon, and listen.
Can you put them in order, from the lowest note to the highest? Try playing a tune!
Let's remember.
Shorter strings make higher notes.
Tighter strings, with more tension, make higher notes too.
Shorter tubes and shorter bars make higher notes.
And when you blow across a bottle, more air makes a lower note.
Rock-star work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.
